evergreen_facts.text: Mumbai was built on seven islands that land reclamation gradually joined into a single landmass.
Portugal handed Bombay to England in 1661 as part of Catherine of Braganza's dowry when she married Charles II.
Bombay was officially renamed Mumbai in 1995, though both names remain in everyday use.
The Bombay Stock Exchange in Mumbai, founded in 1875, is the oldest stock exchange in Asia.
The Gateway of India, an arch completed in 1924, looks out over Mumbai Harbour from Apollo Bunder.
Mumbai's Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, a Victorian Gothic railway station, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The Elephanta Caves, on an island in Mumbai Harbour, contain ancient rock-cut temples devoted to Shiva.
Mumbai's seafront Marine Drive is nicknamed the Queen's Necklace for its curve of streetlights at night.
Mumbai is the center of the Hindi-language film industry, known around the world as Bollywood.
Mumbai's dabbawalas deliver home-cooked lunches to office workers using a system of painted codes.
During Ganesh Chaturthi, Mumbai carries huge idols of Ganesha through the streets to be immersed in the sea.
Vada pav, a spiced potato fritter tucked into a bread roll, is Mumbai's signature street food.
Pav bhaji, a spiced vegetable mash eaten with buttered bread rolls, originated in Mumbai.
Sanjay Gandhi National Park lies inside Mumbai's city limits and holds the ancient Buddhist Kanheri Caves.
Mumbai gets most of its yearly rain from the southwest monsoon, which arrives in June and lasts until September.
Mumbai's Wankhede Stadium hosted the 2011 Cricket World Cup final, which India won.
